proof.text: Put $X=\operatorname{Spec}C$. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-localization-away-basic-open], the $D(f)$ form a basis and $D(f)\cong\operatorname{Spec}C_f$ topologically. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact], each such spectrum and $X$ are quasi-compact. Also $D(f)\cap D(g)=D(fg)$. Every quasi-compact open is a finite union of these basic opens, so intersections of two quasi-compact opens are finite unions of quasi-compact basic opens. Thus $X$ satisfies all three hypotheses of the component-intersection theorem used next.

source.place: Tags 00E4 (lemma-standard-open), 00E8 (lemma-quasi-compact), 04PM (lemma-topology-spec); explicit verification of the hypotheses of Topology 005F

proof.text: Fix a connected component $Z$. By [lem-weil-pbc-quasicompact-components-clopen-intersection], $Z$ is the intersection of the clopen neighbourhoods of any of its points. Each such clopen contains all of $Z$, since $Z$ is connected. By [lem-weil-pbc-spec-clopen-idempotent], these neighbourhoods are precisely $D(e)$ for idempotents $e$ with $Z\subseteq D(e)$. Thus $\bigcap_eD(e)=\bigcap_eV(1-e)=V(I_Z)$: the $1-e$ are exactly the idempotents vanishing on $Z$. Prime ideals of $C/I_Z$ correspond to primes of $C$ containing $I_Z$, with the same induced Zariski topology, proving the asserted underlying space. Moreover $C_Z=\varinjlim_e C_e$, with the idempotents indexed by reverse inclusion of $D(e)$ and transition to $C_{ee'}$ from $C_e,C_{e'}$. Indeed $C_e=C/(1-e)$: inverting an idempotent makes it equal to $1$. These quotient maps are surjective and their directed union of kernels is exactly $I_Z$: for finitely many idempotents $d_i$ vanishing on $Z$, $e=\prod_i(1-d_i)$ equals $1$ on $Z$ and kills every $d_i$. Thus every finite sum of multiples of the $d_i$ dies at this stage; conversely every kernel $(1-e)$ lies in $I_Z$. This proves the colimit assertion directly by the universal property of a quotient.

source.place: Tag 00EG (lemma-connected-component), proof from Topology 005F and Algebra 00EE; explicit quotient-colimit calculation

proof.text: Assume (ii), and let the family in (i) be given. Refine its members by affine etale charts $V=\operatorname{Spec}B\to X$: an affine open of $U_a$ composed with $U_a\to X$ is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-composition-cancellation], clauses (1) and (2), and these charts still jointly cover $X$. For each $Z$, its closed point maps to a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $C$. Choose a point $y$ of one chart $V$ above $\mathfrak p$. Since $I_Z\subseteq\mathfrak p$, the map $C\to\kappa(y)$ factors through $C_Z$, giving a point of $V\times_X\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$ over the closed point. The base change is etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-ring-base-change]. Applying [lem-sbc-strict-henselian-etale-neighbourhood-section] to that point gives a section over all of $\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$, equivalently, by the affine scheme/ring correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum], a $C_Z$-algebra map $C_Z\otimes_CB\to C_Z$, i.e. a $C$-algebra map $B\to C_Z$. By [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-finite-presentation-localization], $B$ is a finitely presented $C$-algebra. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-finite-presentation-algebra-factors-filtered-colimit] with base ring $C$ and the small directed system $C_e$ of step 2. The map factors as $B\to C_e\to C_Z$ for one idempotent $e$ with $Z\subseteq D(e)$. The first map is a $C$-algebra map, so it is a section $D(e)=\operatorname{Spec}C_e\to V$ over $X$. In particular its composite to the original member $U_a$ is a section over this clopen neighbourhood of the whole component, not merely a section over the component quotient.

source.place: Tag 00QO (lemma-characterize-finite-presentation), (1) implies (3), and Tag 00U2 (lemma-etale); strict-local section input as stated in the cited project node

proof.text: The clopens $D(e)$ obtained in step 3 cover every component and hence $X$. Quasi-compactness from [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact] gives a finite subcover $W_1,\ldots,W_n$. Put $P_1=W_1$ and $P_j=W_j\setminus\bigcup_{i<j}W_i$. The $P_j$ are pairwise disjoint clopens with union $X$, each contained in $W_j$. Restrict the section on $W_j$ to $P_j$, and compose it with the chosen inclusion $U_{a(j)}\to\coprod_a U_a$. These maps glue over the disjoint open covering $\{P_j\}$ to a morphism from $X$ to the coproduct whose composite to $X$ is the identity on every $P_j$, hence is the identity. This proves (i). If $C=0$, $X$ is empty and its unique map to the covering coproduct is already a section.

source.place: Tag 00E8 (lemma-quasi-compact); elementary finite disjoint refinement and gluing of scheme morphisms

proof.text: Assume (i), and fix a component $Z$. For $\bar f\in C_Z$, choose a lift $f\in C$. The two maps $\operatorname{Spec}C_f\to X$ and $\operatorname{Spec}C_{1-f}\to X$ are etale by [lem-weil-pbc-etale-algebra-finite-presentation-localization], clause (2) applied to the identity $C\to C$, and their images are $D(f),D(1-f)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-spec-localization-away-basic-open]. They cover $X$. A section provided by (i) partitions $X$ into the inverse images of the two summands, which are clopen. Connectedness forces the nonempty $Z$ to lie wholly in one part; the section identity then forces $Z\subseteq D(f)$ or $Z\subseteq D(1-f)$. By step 2, $D(\bar f)=\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$ or $D(1-\bar f)=\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$, so [lem-weil-pbc-spec-basic-opens-unit-ideal-quasi-compact], clause (ii), shows that $\bar f$ or $1-\bar f$ is a unit. Hence $C_Z$ is local: two distinct maximal ideals would give $u+v=1$ with $u$ in the first and $v$ in the second, contradicting this unit alternative for $u$. A maximal ideal exists because $\operatorname{Spec}C_Z=Z$ is nonempty.

source.place: Tag 00U2 (lemma-etale), localizations; Tags 00E4 and 00E0; agent argument deriving locality from the split Zariski cover

proof.text: For every faithfully flat etale $C$-algebra $B$, [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum] says $\operatorname{Spec}B\to X$ is surjective. Apply (i) to this singleton family to obtain a section. The affine scheme/ring correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] turns it into a $C$-algebra retraction $B\to C$. Therefore [lem-weil-pbc-split-etale-covers-maximal-local-criterion], applied to $C$ itself, implies that $C_{\mathfrak m}$ is strictly henselian for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset C$. No cover-splitting assumption on a quotient of $C$ has been invoked.

Let $\mathfrak n$ be the unique maximal ideal of $C_Z$ from step 5 and $\mathfrak m$ its inverse image in $C$. The quotient map makes $\mathfrak m$ maximal. Each idempotent generator $d$ of $I_Z$ lies in $\mathfrak m$, so $1-d\notin\mathfrak m$; since $d(1-d)=0$, $d$ becomes zero in $C_{\mathfrak m}$. Thus $C\to C_{\mathfrak m}$ factors through $C_Z$. Conversely every $s\notin\mathfrak m$ maps outside $\mathfrak n$ and is a unit in the local ring $C_Z$, so the quotient map extends to $C_{\mathfrak m}\to C_Z$ by the fraction construction [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. These maps are inverse: both composites fix the images of $C$, and fractions are determined by those images and inverses of denominators. Hence $C_Z\cong C_{\mathfrak m}$, which is strictly henselian by step 6. This proves (ii), completing the equivalence without treating locality as part of the component-ring construction.

title: Affine split-etale-cover criterion in terms of strictly henselian components
statement: For a commutative ring $C$ and a connected component $Z$ of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], its component ring is $C_Z=C/I_Z$, where $I_Z$ is generated by the idempotents $e\in C$ with $Z\subseteq V(e)$; the canonical closed subscheme $\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$ has underlying space $Z$. The following conditions are equivalent: (i) for every jointly surjective family of etale morphisms $\{U_a\to\operatorname{Spec}C\}_{a\in A}$ on the small etale site [def-weil-pbc-etale-site], the map $\coprod_{a\in A}U_a\to\operatorname{Spec}C$ has a section; (ii) every component ring $C_Z$ is strictly henselian local [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. The section in (i) may meet different summands on different open-and-closed subsets of the base. Neither a finite number of components nor openness of individual components is assumed.

source.place: Hübner–Schmidt, The tame site of a scheme, §6 component-ring convention (printed p. 12), Definition 7.8 (printed p. 14) and Proposition 7.9, etale case (printed p. 15), citing Artin, On the joins of Hensel rings, Proposition 3.2. A covering family is read as its disjoint-union covering morphism.
